tier_reason: The README's 'Comparison against CGAL' section compares against CGAL's Alpha_wrap_3 and gives one summary figure ('ours ~2x faster on most inputs in this GMP-free CGAL environment') with no per-model timings, hardware or compiler. The comparison tool (tools/cgal_wrap, aw_metrics) is public, but methodology is partial and the measurement is first-party, so C.

corrections.caveats: One summary sentence ('competitive to faster, ~2x faster on most inputs') with no timing table; the CGAL reference is built GMP-free (CGAL 6.x fetched by CMake with -DAW_CGAL_REFERENCE=ON), which can make CGAL slower than a typical GMP-backed install; hardware and compiler unstated. The benchmarks/thingi10k README reports robustness (1000/1000 valid wraps) and absolute times (median 1.1 s, p90 6.2 s, max 59 s per model, 32-way parallel) but no CGAL timings. Output is coarser (0.6-1.0x CGAL's face count), so equal work is not shown. Very new repo (first commit 2026-07-29, 8 commits, 10 stars) and every commit lists Claude as co-author. Not an independent measurement.

notes: README numbers match the record. Metadata checked on the repo page: MIT, 10 stars, not a fork, last commit 2026-08-31. CGAL is a named incumbent of geometry-spatial, so baseline_in_list true is right.

tier_reason: Both suites publish code. cmpute/storage-spatial-index-benchmark is third-party but states no compiler, flags or CPU (Ubuntu 20.04 WSL2 only). mloskot/spatial_index_benchmark states VC++ 11.0 32-bit and a Xeon E5-2687W, but not its flags, and its authors are Boost.Geometry developers. Neither reaches A or B, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: cmpute suite (Ubuntu 20.04 WSL2), README logs: 100,000-box insertion 0.19517 ms/box (Boost, mmap file) vs 0.8756 (libspatialindex) and 0.44314 (SQLite R*Tree), about 4.5x and 2.3x (derived from page data); query at 10,000 boxes 0.0217 vs 0.2852 and 0.6142 ms/box, about 13x and 28x (derived from page data); file size 6,190,608 B vs 25,821,184 B and 8,536,064 B. SQLite was faster than Boost on insertion at 1,000 boxes (0.03 vs 0.184 ms/box) and 10,000 boxes (0.0301 vs 0.2023). mloskot suite, results/2/*.dat (1M random boxes, 100K intersection queries, max node capacity 4-200, seconds): bulk-loaded R* load 1.06-1.39 s (bgi) vs 5.13-6.90 s (lsi STR); queries on the bulk-loaded tree 0.050-0.126 s vs 1.55-6.36 s; iterative R* load 2.95-12.95 s vs 24.4-107.8 s; iterative linear queries 1.26-3.30 s vs 16.8-132.3 s.
corrections.caveats: Boost.Geometry is itself one of this category's named incumbents (spec: Boost.Geometry, CGAL, GEOS, R-tree baselines), so the entry only claims its R-tree beats libspatialindex and SQLite R*Tree. cmpute repo: archived 2024-05-11, no license file, 2 stars. Its CMakeLists sets no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE, so a default build has no optimization flags. Its timer is std::chrono::system_clock truncated to whole milliseconds. The Boost tree lives in a Boost.Interprocess managed_mapped_file, so its storage is not strictly file-based as libspatialindex's is. In benchmark_boost.cpp the query checksum accumulator (uint64_t result) is never initialized, so the logged checksums are meaningless and result equality is not shown. mloskot repo: BSL-1.0, 50 stars, last commit 2019-07-07. Its authors (Mateusz Loskot, Adam Wulkiewicz) are Boost.Geometry developers, it calls itself a non-academic first prototype that may have bugs, and it used 2013-era library versions. Exact values are in results/2/*.dat.

notes: Per the orchestrator's instruction this is the category's baseline itself (Boost.Geometry, same repo URL), so it is filed as known-project. The numbers do check out against libspatialindex and SQLite R*Tree if you prefer to keep it as a reference entry: use the corrected claimed_speedup (exact .dat values replace chart read-offs) and caveats. Repo metadata checked: BSL-1.0, 516 stars, last develop commit 2026-08-17.

tier_reason: The README benchmark tables against Clipper match the record and state compiler (MSVC 2019 19.24.28314 x64) and CPU (i7-6700K). The benchmark code is public in this repo (tests/benchmarks/clipperbenchmarks.cpp and offsetbenchmarks.cpp, Google Benchmark), but optimization flags and build type are not stated, so not A. First-party, so C; the >50x arcs-exact ratios with unstated flags also cap it at C.

corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark on about 2019-2020 hardware. The benchmark code is in tests/benchmarks of this repo (clipperbenchmarks.cpp; Clipper is fetched by tests/benchmarks/clipper.cmake from the author's jbuckmccready/clipper-lib mirror at origin/master, so the Clipper version is not pinned). Optimization flags and build type are not stated. Most of the large ratios come from keeping arcs exact instead of approximating them, a different representation from Clipper's. With arcs approximated for both, the result is close: at 1e-2, 1.0x on the circle, 0.7x on BM_Profile1 and 0.9x on BM_Profile2; at 1e-3, 0.9x on BM_Profile1. The author says the C++ version is no longer actively developed (the Rust cavalier_contours replaces it) and the last commit was 2024-08-28.

notes: All quoted ratios and timings match the README tables. Metadata from the repo page: MIT, 515 stars, not a fork or archived, last commit 2024-08-28 (stale). Clipper is not a spec-named incumbent but is the de facto polygon-offsetting library, so it is a recognizable baseline.
